source.title: Memory-based Language Models: An Efficient, Explainable, and Eco-friendly Approach to Large Language Modeling
source.citation: A. van den Bosch et al., 2025
source.authors: A. van den Bosch; A. Paton; Teun Buijse; P. Berck; M. van Gompel

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends learning-curve analysis to memory-based language models and reports how next-token accuracy changes with training-data size. It does not measure the cross-entropy-loss or compute-allocation claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports next-token accuracy learning curves, not held-out cross-entropy loss. Its comparisons with GPT variants and its perplexity analysis do not test the listed versions: the perplexity calculation excludes tokens assigned zero probability. The learning-curve accuracy findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study measures next-token accuracy learning curves of non-neural memory-based (k-NN/decision-tree) models, not held-out cross-entropy loss of neural LMs. Its perplexity excludes tokens given zero probability, so it is not a held-out loss either. It cites Kaplan et al. only to contrast scaling dimensions. No version is tested. The record's 'tests'/T3 label contradicts its own finding that every version is not_tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors also stress that the main contribution is efficiency: about 1,000x lower training CO2, 10-100x lower inference cost, transparency and memorization. They say performance grows 'approximately log-linearly with more data, or better' and that model size scales linearly.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates memory-based k-NN and decision-tree language models, rather than fitting neural-model held-out loss against parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported token-accuracy curve bends around one billion training tokens; fitting the whole range versus measurements from one billion tokens upwards gives different slopes and extrapolations. Context width also changes the observed accuracy curves.

fits_no_version.finding: TRIBL2 accuracy fit over the whole range: r=0.9935, +4.1% per 10x data, 39.2% projected at 1T tokens. Fit on the five points at 1B tokens and above: r=0.9993, +7.3% per 10x, 47.7% projected. The curve bends around 1B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For memory-based LMs, next-token accuracy rises roughly log-linearly with data, and the extrapolation depends on the fitted range.

fits_no_version.finding: At context width 1, accuracy tapers off near 16%. Widths 3 to 5 keep rising and hardly differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memory-based LM accuracy learning curves depend on context width.

record.problems: The scaling results use next-token accuracy rather than held-out cross-entropy loss. The paper reports a bend in the curve and leaves its cause unresolved; the post-bend fit uses five measurements. The authors also note that later flattening cannot be ruled out and that their models are restricted to a four-token context in the main experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were left out for the listed claim versions. The paper's plotted learning-curve values for additional training-set sizes and OLIFANT variants, and its GPT comparisons, are not catalogued as version-linked results because they report accuracy rather than the measures named in the versions.

untested.parts: No held-out cross-entropy loss versus parameters, tokens or compute for neural LMs.
Extrapolates accuracy for a memory-based model, not neural pretraining loss.
No compute-optimal allocation; in memory-based models, model size and compute are tied to data.
No variation of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime with loss power laws.
No loss exponents or compute-optimal splits whose dependence on fitting choices could be compared.

record.verdict_notes: The Figure 10 perplexity curves (OLIFANT versus GPT-2/GPT-Neo) are not held-out loss, because zero-probability tokens are excluded; they are rightly not linked to any version. The GPT-2/GPT-Neo points are pretrained models used as comparators, not a scaling test by this study. Relation changed from 'tests' to 'discusses' (T6).

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out cross-entropy loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
It extrapolates token prediction accuracy, not held-out loss from small runs to much larger runs.
It does not vary parameter count and training tokens under fixed compute or estimate a compute-optimal allocation.
It varies memory-model context width, not depth, width, or other neural architecture details at fixed parameter count.
It studies text next-token prediction in memory-based models, not the listed other modalities or training regimes.
It does not measure downstream-task performance or predict it from pretraining loss.
It reports a bend in next-token accuracy versus training-data size, but does not test dependence of held-out-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: TRIBL2
rows.stage_stated: memory-based language model trained on EduFineWeb data
rows.operation_detail: Fit log-linear regression to token prediction accuracy over the full range of training-set sizes.

conditions.value: first 10 thousand lines of EduFineWeb validation subcorpus; 512,660 tokens

rows.value: r = 0.9935; Token prediction accuracy = -0.1006 + 0.0178 × ln(Training set size); increase of 4.1% with every 10-fold increase; estimated 39.2% at 1 trillion tokens
rows.note: This is an accuracy curve and extrapolation, not a held-out cross-entropy-loss result.
rows.check: Accuracy log-linear fit for a memory-based model; no version names this measure or system. Link and state are correct.

rows.subject: TRIBL2
rows.stage_stated: memory-based language model trained on EduFineWeb data
rows.operation_detail: Fit a log-linear regression to the measurements at and above 1 billion training tokens.

conditions.value: first 10 thousand lines of EduFineWeb validation subcorpus; 512,660 tokens
measurements from 1 billion training tokens upwards; five measurements

rows.value: r = 0.9993; Token prediction accuracy = -0.3960 + 0.0316 × ln(Training set size); increase of 7.3% with every 10-fold increase; estimated 47.7% at 1 trillion tokens
rows.note: The fitted slope and extrapolated accuracy differ from the whole-range fit; these are not loss exponents.
rows.check: The text calls this a 'logistic regression', but the equation is log-linear. The fit uses only five points. Not a loss law; link is correct.

rows.subject: TRIBL2
rows.stage_stated: memory-based language model trained on EduFineWeb data
rows.operation_detail: Measure next-token prediction accuracy as training-set size increases across context widths.

conditions.value: increasing sizes, from 10,000 lines with increments of factor 10, up to 100 million training instances

rows.value: The curve starts with the highest accuracy and tapers off at about 16%.
rows.note: The text also says context widths 3, 4, and 5 continue increasing while hardly differing; plotted values are not transcribed here.
rows.check: Context-width accuracy curves (Figure 4) for TRIBL2. Not a loss or neural-architecture result; link is correct.
